data.heading: Publish your site. Run your business. Prove it all works.
data.summary: Kumwe is a new kind of CMS and application platform that's built human-led but AI-assisted. Every page on this site is managed content served by the system it describes.

features.heading: Content that stays governed.
features.body:
Every page on this site is a managed record: its content type pins the fields, its workflow state decides public visibility, and its menu item gives it a canonical route. The layout is driven by the document itself, so editors fill defined fields rather than hand-building markup. You are reading the result now.

[Explore managed content](/content)

features.heading: Business applications from typed definitions.
features.body:
State fields, relationships, actions, exposure, and lifecycle in a versioned business definition, and Kumwe compiles it into portable storage, shared record services, and generated screens, APIs, and reports. Every surface reads the same policy-aware record boundary, so a rule changed in the definition changes everywhere at once.

[Model a business application](/business)

features.heading: Least privilege, down to the field.
features.body:
Capabilities, row policies, and field disclosure rules decide what each actor may see and do, and missing context defaults to denial. Sensitive operations can require independent maker and checker approval, and ordinary users work in a separate [portal](/portal) that creates its own authenticated context and exposes only trusted routes and generated surfaces.

[See the security model](/business/security)

features.heading: Extensions without a second pipeline.
features.body:
Signed extension manifests contribute routes, services, business definitions, events, jobs, and templates through stable registries, and the site operator decides what authority each package is granted. Integrations call the same services through REST, the command line, and MCP, behind one shared authorization boundary.

[Extend and integrate](/extend)

features.heading: Operations you can prove.
features.body:
Health endpoints gate startup, workers and schedules run durable jobs, and backup, restore, and upgrade are rehearsed rather than assumed. Releases qualify against MariaDB, MySQL, and PostgreSQL before they ship, and the same evidence-first checks are documented for your own deployments.

[Operate Kumwe](/operate)

closing.heading: Open in purpose, curated in implementation.
closing.body: Kumwe welcomes use cases, testing, demonstration profiles, extension ideas, documentation, and domain knowledge. Core code moves through a controlled maintainer pipeline so releases stay coherent and safe — you always know where your contribution plugs in and who carries it from there. Begin with [Start here](/start-here), then sign in with the [demonstration accounts](/start-here/demo-access) to try every role in the running example.

data.heading: Turn a running Kumwe installation into a known baseline.
data.summary: Confirm health, sign in with the owner account, and complete one small publishing loop before configuring deeper business behavior.
data.body:
## Recommended first loop
- Confirm that the readiness endpoint reports success.
- Sign in at the [administrator](/administrator) with the owner created during installation.
- Open Content, edit a demonstration page, and save it.
- Use its workflow transition to keep it published.
- Open the public path and confirm the edited content and navigation.
- Return to the dashboard and inspect recent activity.

This loop proves the web runtime, database, session, authorization, content revision, rendering, and public routing boundaries together. Keep the change small so a failure points to one boundary.

capabilities.heading: Know what success looks like.
capabilities.body: A healthy first run has working readiness, administrator assets, a signed-in owner, editable pages, a nominated homepage, and a main menu. Business, portal, extension, and automation features can then be explored without confusing installation problems with configuration problems.

platform.heading: Continue by outcome.
platform.body: Use [Content](/content) when the goal is publishing, [Business applications](/business) when the goal is structured operations, [Extend Kumwe](/extend) for packages and integrations, or [Operate Kumwe](/operate) for deployment and recovery.

data.heading: Start the complete local runtime and create its owner.
data.summary: Kumwe targets PHP 8.5 and supports MariaDB LTS, MySQL 8.4, and PostgreSQL 17 with Redis for runtime coordination.
data.body:
## Before startup
- Copy the example environment file and choose an unused local HTTP port.
- Keep database credentials, application secrets, and the owner password outside source control.
- Install the locked Composer and frontend dependencies through the documented development container.

## Bring the installation online
- Run the portable database migrations.
- Create the first owner with the user management command.
- Start the application, web, database, and Redis services.
- Check both liveness and readiness before opening the user interface.

## Verify the result
The public homepage should render managed database content, the administrator should load its committed assets, and the owner should be able to sign in. If one of those checks fails, inspect the service health and logs before changing content or permissions. The [administrator tour](/start-here/administrator) is the next step once this baseline passes.

platform.heading: Keep the database choice portable.
platform.body: Use the documented connection variables for the selected driver and run the same migrations and tests. Kumwe treats MariaDB, MySQL, and PostgreSQL as supported targets, so installation behavior must not depend on one database dialect.

data.heading: Navigate by the task you are authorized to perform.
data.summary: The administrator hides unavailable areas and applies the same capability checks used by API, CLI, MCP, and background operations.
data.body:
## Main work areas
- Dashboard summarizes content, recent activity, extensions, and system state.
- Content, Media, Navigation, and Settings shape the public site.
- Content models define editorial fields and workflow states.
- Business definitions and schema plans create transactional applications.
- Business workspaces and Reports expose live records and governed projections.
- Access and Business security manage capabilities, policies, membership, approvals, tokens, and stronger authentication.
- Extensions and Automation manage installed contributions and durable background work.

A missing navigation item usually means the signed-in actor lacks its capability. Do not work around that by editing tables. Grant the narrow role or scoped permission through Access, sign in again if the security epoch changed, and verify the intended screen appears.

capabilities.heading: Use a reversible tour.
capabilities.body: Start by viewing lists, then edit one demonstration record with its displayed version. Avoid changing owner access, deleting extensions, or executing a schema plan until you have reviewed the confirmation screen and recovery path.

data.heading: Model content once and publish it through governed paths.
data.summary: Pages, content types, workflows, media, navigation, and presentation settings form one editable public site rather than separate page-builder data.
data.body:
Use [Pages and publishing](/content/pages) for day-to-day editorial work, [Content models and workflows](/content/models) when the fields or lifecycle must change, and [Media, navigation, and presentation](/content/media-navigation) when the public chrome and routes must change.

All three areas meet at a published content record. Its type pins validation, its workflow state decides public visibility, its menu item gives it a canonical route, and site settings may nominate it as the homepage.

capabilities.heading: A dependable editorial loop.
capabilities.body: Create a draft, fill the defined fields, save with the current version, transition through an allowed workflow action, and verify the public route. Each write creates audit evidence and a revision snapshot.

platform.heading: Managed content stays reusable.
platform.body: The site template receives presented content, while REST, CLI, and MCP receive structured records. Keep meaning in fields and the content body so another delivery surface can reuse it without scraping rendered HTML.

data.heading: Create, review, publish, revise, and retire managed content.
data.summary: Every entry pins its content-type and workflow versions, carries an optimistic version, and records immutable revision snapshots.
data.body:
## Create a page
- Open Content and choose New content.
- Select Page or another published content type.
- Enter a clear title, stable URL slug, and the fields shown by its schema.
- Save the draft before adding it to navigation.

## Publish safely
- Use only a transition offered by the pinned workflow.
- Confirm any publication window includes the current time.
- Add the page to a menu or nominate it as the homepage when it is meant to be public.
- Open its canonical path in a signed-out browser.

## Revise or retire
Save edits with the displayed version so concurrent changes cannot be silently overwritten. Each accepted edit records an immutable revision and an audit event. Trash or restore through the managed actions; references such as the homepage and navigation targets are protected from becoming broken pointers.

platform.heading: Use the supported rich-text vocabulary.
platform.body: Bodies accept plain paragraphs, second-level headings, bullet lists, bold text, and safe links. Store no raw HTML. Fragments, root-relative paths, and approved web or email links are rendered safely; unsafe targets remain visible as text.

data.heading: Define fields and lifecycle rules before editors depend on them.
data.summary: Published content types and workflows are immutable versions, so existing entries remain interpretable while a model evolves.
data.body:
## Content types
A content type has a stable handle, name, field schema, workflow reference, and published version. Use required fields only for information every editor can supply. Prefer structured fields for values another surface must filter or display consistently, and use rich text for narrative content.

## Workflows
A workflow defines states, the initial state, which states are public, and the transitions allowed between them. Name transitions as actions an editor understands. Keep review and publication authority separate where governance requires it.

## Evolve without ambiguity
Draft a new definition, validate it, and publish a new version rather than rewriting a version already used by content. Entries retain the type and workflow versions that validated them. Test old and new entries through the administrator and public renderer before making the new model the normal authoring choice.

capabilities.heading: This guide is Page v3 content.
capabilities.body: The demonstration pages use the current Page schema: optional hero identity, heading, summary, actions, a required rich-text body, and two optional anchored sections. Editing these fixtures therefore exercises the same model an operator sees.

data.heading: Connect reusable assets, canonical routes, and validated presentation settings.
data.summary: Media, menu targets, homepage selection, branding, and accessible color schemes stay independently manageable.
data.body:
## Media
Upload supported images and documents through [Media](/administrator/media). Kumwe records identity, file metadata, checksum, and ownership, then serves the asset through a managed media URL. Choose an existing asset from a media-aware field instead of copying files into the public directory.

## Navigation
Build menus in [Navigation](/administrator/navigation). A menu item targets managed content, an anchor on managed content, or a safe custom URL. Parent and position create the public hierarchy; content identity stays stable even when a slug or path changes. This documentation menu intentionally uses only one parent and one child level.

## Settings and presentation
Use [Site settings](/administrator/settings) to nominate a published Page as the homepage, choose the primary menu, set locale and timezone, control indexing, and configure presentation. Logos must use safe root-relative URLs. Button and header styles use fixed choices, and every color scheme must satisfy the complete palette and text-contrast rules.

capabilities.heading: Verify from a signed-out browser.
capabilities.body: After changing a menu, homepage, logo, or palette, open the public site without an administrator session. Check the root path, one nested route, keyboard navigation, mobile layout, readable contrast, and a missing optional image.

data.heading: Turn business definitions into governed transactional workspaces.
data.summary: Kumwe compiles versioned definitions into portable storage, shared record services, generated surfaces, policies, approvals, reports, and integration events.
data.body:
A business application begins with a definition, not a generated screen. The definition states fields, relationships, exposure, actions, reports, and lifecycle. A reviewed schema plan materializes its physical storage. The runtime then exposes one policy-aware record boundary to the administrator, portal, REST, CLI, MCP, workers, and extensions.

Use [Business definitions](/business/definitions) to model it, [Records and generated surfaces](/business/records) to run it, and [Security, approvals, and portal](/business/security) to bound who may see or change it.

capabilities.heading: Build in the safe order.
capabilities.body: Publish the definition, review the generated plan, capture required recovery evidence, approve and execute the plan, create a small record set, then add broader exposure and integration. Security policy should be tested before real data enters the system.

platform.heading: Keep one source of truth.
platform.body: Generated screens are projections of the published definition and shared services. Do not patch a generated route or database table to add a business rule. Change the definition or application policy so all surfaces receive the same behavior.

data.heading: Publish a complete, versioned contract for records and surfaces.
data.summary: Definitions describe identity, fields, defaults, indexes, relationships, exposure, actions, approvals, reports, and extension ownership.
data.body:
## Draft the smallest useful model
- Give the definition a stable lowercase handle and a clear singular and plural name.
- Choose field types that match the business value, including money, quantities, dates, references, media, choices, and rich text.
- Mark identity, required, searchable, sortable, filterable, and visible behavior deliberately.
- Add relationships and ownership only when their lifecycle is understood.
- Declare exposure and actions explicitly; omitted surfaces stay unavailable.

## Validate and publish
Kumwe rejects unknown keys, invalid expressions, unsafe dependency cycles, incompatible relationship targets, and contracts that exceed bounded budgets. Publishing creates an immutable definition version and dependency graph. Later changes become a new draft and version.

## Review extension contributions
A signed manifest can contribute definitions, fields, actions, reports, events, jobs, and policies, but the package cannot silently grant itself operator authority. Inspect ownership and lifecycle behavior before activation.

platform.heading: Materialize through a schema plan.
platform.body: After publication, move to [Records and generated surfaces](/business/records). Generate a plan, read every operation and risk, provide recovery evidence where required, then approve and execute it through the guarded plan lifecycle.

data.heading: Apply a reviewed schema plan, then use the same record service everywhere.
data.summary: Generated lists, forms, details, relationships, history, actions, reports, REST, CLI, and MCP all compile from one published definition.
data.body:
## Materialize storage
Generate the schema plan for a published definition. Review its exact portable operations, risk classification, and recovery requirements. Capture recovery evidence, approve the expected plan version, execute it once, and inspect its durable result before creating records.

## Work with records
Use the generated workspace to create, list, filter, sort, view, relate, update, transition, and review history. Mutations carry the displayed record version; stale writes fail instead of replacing concurrent work. Collection queries have bounded page size, filter depth, relation fan-out, and include budgets.

## Compare surfaces
Perform one read in the administrator and compare it with REST, CLI, or MCP. Fields omitted by exposure or disclosure policy must stay omitted everywhere. Repeat a mutation with its idempotency key to confirm it replays the original outcome rather than writing twice.

Reports and exports use the same policy-safe query boundary and record enough metadata and checksums to make their result explainable.

capabilities.heading: Disable before destructive lifecycle work.
capabilities.body: Definition disablement stops new runtime use without erasing data. Uninstall and purge require explicit checks, retention decisions, dependency handling, and recovery evidence. Never treat a generated table as disposable because its screen can be regenerated.

data.heading: Decide which rows, fields, actions, and scopes each actor may use.
data.summary: Capabilities begin the decision; site ownership, organization and workspace membership, row policy, field disclosure, approvals, step-up proofs, and token scope finish it.
data.body:
## Establish scope
Create only the organizations, workspaces, and memberships the workflow needs. Grant capabilities at the narrowest supported scope. A capability never bypasses site ownership, membership, record policy, or field disclosure.

## Protect records and fields
Row policies use a closed conditional language and default to denial when required context is missing. Field rules control display, detail, create, update, search, filter, sort, report, relation, and public-reference use independently. A hidden field must also be non-queryable where inference would disclose it.

## Separate sensitive decisions
Bind selected operations to maker and checker approval rules. The requester cannot satisfy an independent approval requirement alone. Stronger operations consume a one-time step-up proof, and scoped tokens cannot exceed the issuing actor or delegated boundary.

## Verify the ordinary-user portal
The portal creates its own authenticated context and exposes only trusted contributed routes and generated surfaces. Test permitted and forbidden organizations, workspaces, rows, fields, actions, approvals, and stale sessions. Administrator visibility is not evidence that portal policy is correct.

capabilities.heading: Keep the decision reconstructable.
capabilities.body: Review audit events and authorization evidence after a sensitive test. The record should identify actor, scope, action, policy outcome, resource, version, approval or step-up use, and a sanitized failure reason without exposing secrets or raw request bodies.

data.heading: Package new behavior without creating a second application pipeline.
data.summary: Signed extension manifests contribute services, routes, business definitions, events, jobs, reports, policies, templates, assets, and migrations through stable registries.
data.body:
Use an extension when behavior must be installed, versioned, verified, disabled, upgraded, and removed as a unit. Keep domain rules and application services independent of delivery. Register contributions through the provider and the supported extension APIs instead of locating the container from ordinary classes.

Use [Extensions and templates](/extend/extensions) for package structure, lifecycle, routes, assets, and presentation. Use [Integrations and automation](/extend/integrations) for events, inbox delivery, jobs, schedules, process managers, reports, and projections.

capabilities.heading: Treat installable code as a trust boundary.
capabilities.body: Verify the package signature, checksums, manifest schema, compatibility, asset inventory, migration plan, capabilities, and ownership before activation. Contributions declare what a package requests; the site operator still decides what authority is granted.

platform.heading: Design the exit before the install.
platform.body: State what disablement stops, which data survives uninstall, when purge is allowed, how queued work drains, how migrations recover, and how a backup restores the extension-owned graph. Exercise those paths in conformance tests.

data.heading: Scaffold, build, verify, install, and recover a complete component.
data.summary: Manifest schema 4 binds package identity, compatibility, checksums, services, contributions, assets, migrations, and lifecycle declarations.
data.body:
## Build the package
Start from the complete-component scaffold and keep its namespace, package identifier, manifest, provider, tests, and documentation aligned. Declare only supported manifest keys. Inventory every runtime asset and migration, lock dependencies, and make the build reproducible.

## Contribute behavior
The provider may register services while it has the container, but ordinary classes receive dependencies through constructors. Routes call application services. Business definitions, fields, actions, reports, events, jobs, schedules, policies, administrator links, portal routes, and settings use their typed contribution registries.

## Manage lifecycle
Run static and lifecycle conformance before install. Review the plan, install, activate, disable, reactivate, upgrade, uninstall, and restore from backup. Interrupted activation must leave the previous active runtime intact.

## Templates
A template package owns Twig files, declared assets, compatibility, and presentation behavior. It consumes already-presented data and must not bypass content, authorization, or settings services. Verify homepage, nested routes, missing optional fields, errors, responsive layouts, keyboard use, contrast, security headers, and caching.

capabilities.heading: Study the shipped proof components.
capabilities.body: The repository includes small extension and template examples designed for inspection and conformance. Use them to learn package shape and lifecycle boundaries, then replace example identifiers and behavior rather than copying authority assumptions.

data.heading: Connect systems through versioned events, retry-safe delivery, jobs, and policy-safe reports.
data.summary: Kumwe records integration intent durably so restarts, duplicate delivery, ordering, and terminal failure have explicit outcomes.
data.body:
## Events and delivery
Publish versioned events through the shared transaction and outbox boundary. Consumers accept declared schema versions, persist inbox receipts, enforce idempotency, and classify retries. Partition keys preserve required ordering without serializing unrelated work. Terminal failures remain visible for operator action.

## Jobs and schedules
Contributed job types declare their payload contract, retry behavior, capabilities, and owner. Schedules are durable records with timezone and misfire policy. Workers lease bounded batches and handlers remain safe to retry after a crash. Process managers persist their own state and correlate only the events they own.

## Reports and projections
Reports compile against policy-filtered record sources. Field disclosure applies to columns, filters, grouping, aggregates, exports, and relationships. Projections record source event versions and checkpoints so they can rebuild deterministically.

## Test operational behavior
Exercise duplicate events, key reuse, out-of-order delivery, retry exhaustion, lease expiry, disabled sites, removed extensions, schedule misfires, projection rebuild, and restart. Inspect administrator status and metrics rather than treating a quiet queue as proof of success.

capabilities.heading: Make ownership explicit.
capabilities.body: Every contributed event, consumer, job, schedule, process manager, report, and projection belongs to a package and version. Disablement and uninstall must state how new work stops and what happens to pending or retained state.

data.heading: Automate safely, observe the runtime, and prove recovery before release.
data.summary: REST, CLI, and MCP call the same services; production adds health gates, workers, schedules, backups, verified artifacts, and portable database qualification.
data.body:
## Choose an interface
REST uses bearer tokens, capability checks, bounded requests, idempotency keys for mutations, and optimistic versions with entity tags. The command line exposes installation, health, access, content, navigation, settings, business, extension, automation, and MCP transport tasks. MCP is available over streamable HTTP and local standard input with an explicit tool catalog, safe mutation previews, and the same authorization boundary.

## Run production services
Apply migrations as a one-shot operation before starting web traffic. Run the application and web services plus worker and scheduler where automation is enabled. Keep secrets in deployment secret files, serve only the public root, terminate transport security at the approved boundary, and monitor liveness, readiness, queue age, failures, storage, database, Redis, and audit signals.

## Back up and recover
Back up the database together with media, extension state, runtime files, and metadata. Verify the backup, restore into empty targets, boot the restored site, and exercise public, administrator, business, integration, and extension paths. Repeat for every supported database family.

## Qualify a release
Run the complete quality and deployment gates, browser accessibility and responsive checks, fresh install and upgrade tests, extension conformance, security scans, backup and restore, and artifact verification. Identify a release by source revision, locked dependencies, checksums, image digests, software bill of materials, signatures, and provenance.

capabilities.heading: Prefer observable refusal to silent drift.
capabilities.body: Stale versions, denied policy, unsafe input, incompatible manifests, unavailable dependencies, and failed recovery evidence should produce bounded errors and durable operator evidence. Do not bypass a guard to make a demonstration pass.

platform.heading: Keep the demonstration as a regression surface.
platform.body: After an upgrade, revisit the homepage, one nested content route, one record workspace, one portal denial, one integration status, readiness, and a restored backup. These small checks reveal whether the documented paths still match the application.

content.title: Create and publish your first page

data.heading: Take one page from draft to the public site.
data.summary: Sign in, create a draft in Content, submit it for review, publish it, and open the result — one loop through the governed workflow every page uses.
data.body:
This guide takes one page from nothing to a public URL using only the administrator. You need a running installation from the [installation guide](/start-here/getting-started) and an account holding the content capabilities involved; the owner created during installation holds them all.

## How the workflow behaves
- Every edit creates an immutable revision and an audit event, so no state change loses work.
- The editor offers only the transitions valid for the page's current state and your capabilities.
- A published page is public only after its optional publish date and before its optional unpublish date.

Every step below uses generated screens; routine authoring never requires reading or writing JSON.

steps.heading: Sign in at the administrator.
steps.body: Open [/administrator](/administrator) and sign in with the owner account created during installation, or with any user granted content.create, content.submit, and content.publish. The navigation shows only the areas your account may manage, so if **Content** is missing, review the grants under **Users and access** before continuing. The [administrator tour](/start-here/administrator) explains each area.

steps.heading: Open Content.
steps.body: Choose **Content** in the administrator navigation. The list is searchable, filterable, and paginated, with workflow actions, trash, and restore. The installed documentation pages live here as ordinary managed records — this page included — so you can open one to see a finished example before creating your own.

steps.heading: Create the page and choose its layout.
steps.body: Create a new page and select a content type. This documentation site installs six layouts — Document, Guide, Reference, Questions and answers, Landing page, and Article — and each renders differently on the public site; the page you are reading uses the Guide layout. Your choice generates the editor: text, rich-text, media, and the other field controls come from the content type definition. Give the page a title and a slug, then complete the generated fields. [Content models](/content/models) explains how these definitions are built and versioned.

steps.heading: Save the draft.
steps.body: Saving creates the page in the Draft state. Each edit records an immutable revision and an audit event, and optimistic versions stop an old browser tab from overwriting newer work, so you can revise freely. A draft is never public: the public site serves only published pages inside their publication window.

steps.heading: Submit it for review.
steps.body: Use the **Submit** action to move the draft into Review. The editor lists only valid actions for the current state, so Submit appears while the page is a draft and disappears once it is under review. A reviewer holding content.review can return the page for changes, which moves it back to Draft with its revision history intact. On a fresh installation where you hold every capability yourself, the state change still shows how separate editor and reviewer roles divide the work.

steps.heading: Publish.
steps.body: The **Publish** action moves the page from draft or review to Published and requires content.publish. Publication dates are optional: when set, the page is public only after publish_at and before unpublish_at. **Unpublish** returns a published page to Draft at any time, so publishing is never a one-way door.

steps.heading: View it on the public site.
steps.body: Use the **View page** action in the editor. It appears only when the workflow state and publication window make the page public, and it resolves the same URL the public site uses. An unlinked page answers at its slug; once you add it to a menu under **Navigation**, the menu hierarchy becomes its canonical URL, such as /about-us/contact-details. [Media and navigation](/content/media-navigation) covers menus, and [Pages and publishing](/content/pages) covers the rest of the editorial surface.

outcome.heading: What you now have.
outcome.body: A page you created is live at a public URL, and its complete history — every draft revision, the review transition, the publish action, and the matching audit events — is inspectable in the administrator. You have exercised the same workflow every editor uses and the same application services shared by the REST API, command line, and MCP tools. Continue with [content models](/content/models) to define your own layouts, or open [Content](/content) for the wider publishing tour.

data.heading: Sign in as every demonstrated role without a shared secret.
data.summary: The demonstration provisions five staff accounts and three client organizations, generates every password at provisioning time, and writes the sign-ins exactly once to an owner-only credentials file that is never committed.
data.body:
The demonstration installs a complete cast: five staff accounts that sign in at [the administrator](/administrator) and four portal members spread across three fictional client organizations that sign in at [the portal](/portal). Every address lives in the reserved .example zone, and no password is ever shipped — each one is generated on your installation at provisioning time and written once to a protected credentials file.

The cast itself is declared as data in the VDM business profile's access manifest. The **demo:provision-access** command turns that declaration into real accounts: roles and users through the canonical access-control service under an authenticated administrator, and portal memberships through the Business Security tables with audit records. Signing in as each identity in turn is the fastest way to watch [security policy](/business/security) doing real work.

sections.heading: Why the demonstration never ships a password.
sections.body:
A demonstration that ships a fixed default password would teach the wrong habit and leave a known secret in every installation. Kumwe's demo profiles are data-only: they never contain passwords, tokens, or key material of any kind, and the manifest tests enforce that rule. The access manifest declares identities, roles, and organization memberships — nothing more.

Passwords therefore exist only after you provision, only on your installation, and only in one owner-only file. **demo:provision-access** requires host access and a real administrator's credentials, generates a fresh password for every account it creates, and writes them exactly once. Because provisioning runs through the same access-control and audit services you use yourself, the demonstration cast is created the way any real account is — nothing about it bypasses the system it exists to demonstrate.

sections.heading: Five staff roles with deliberately different reach.
sections.body:
All five staff accounts sign in at [the administrator](/administrator) with addresses on the vdm.example domain, and each carries a deliberately different capability set:

- **accountant@vdm.example** holds the full set of business record operations: browse, read, create, update, workflow transitions and actions, relations, history, exports, and reports.
- **clerk@vdm.example** reads business records and works on managed content — creating, updating, and submitting pages for review — without business write access.
- **bookkeeper@vdm.example** is read-only with evidence duties: browse, read, history, exports, and reports, but no create or update.
- **stockkeeper@vdm.example** maintains records and their relations — browse, read, create, update, relate — without exports, reports, or workflow transitions.
- **sysadmin@vdm.example** configures the platform — users, settings, navigation, themes, extensions, and automation, with read access to business schemas — but holds no business record operations.

Sign in as each in turn and compare which administrator areas and record operations appear. The [administrator tour](/start-here/administrator) shows the same areas from the owner's seat; these five show what least privilege looks like when [record and field policy](/business/security) finishes the decision.

sections.heading: Three client organizations behind the portal.
sections.body:
Three fictional client organizations demonstrate the portal side, each with its own workspace and its own records:

- **Kalahari Health Systems** (kalahari-health) has two members — an operations contact and a finance contact — sharing one company, so you can watch two colleagues reach the same organization from different sign-ins.
- **Desert Bloom Foods** (desert-bloom) has one ordering contact and a pending quotation you can accept to watch a portal workflow action complete.
- **Namib Learning Collective** (namib-learning) has one campus contact.

Each member signs in at [the portal](/portal) and sees only that organization's quotations, invoices, subscriptions, and domains beside the shared product catalogue. Portal members hold record capabilities — browsing, reading, workflow actions, relations, history, exports, and reports — and nothing else: no administrator access, no schema or user administration. [Security, approvals, and portal](/business/security) explains how that boundary is enforced, and when you are ready to create a real organization you follow [provision a client](/business/provision-client) instead of the demonstration cast.

sections.heading: Where your credentials file is.
sections.body:
Where the file lands depends on how you installed:

- **bin/kumwe-install** asks for confirmation, then writes **storage/private/demo-access-credentials.json** inside your installation; the path is excluded from version control and is never committed.
- **tools/production-demo.sh** writes **demo-access-credentials.json** inside its owner-only temporary state directory and prints the exact path when readiness passes. Export **KUMWE_DEMO_ACCESS=false** before running it to skip cast provisioning entirely.
- Running **demo:provision-access** yourself, you choose the destination with **--credentials-file**; the path must be absolute and must not exist yet.

The file is created with owner-only mode 0600, and the generated secrets exist nowhere else besides the command's own output. Treat it like any credential store: use it for the review, keep it out of shared channels, and remove it when the review ends. Running **bash tools/production-demo.sh down** deletes the demonstration stack together with its generated secrets.

sections.heading: Re-provision without breaking anyone's sign-in.
sections.body:
Provisioning is refused while the credentials file already exists — the command tells you to move the file away rather than ever overwriting it. That refusal is the write-once guarantee: no later run can silently rotate or expose credentials a reviewer is already using.

The run itself is idempotent in the safe direction. Already-provisioned identities are confirmed without a password change, so a rerun never invalidates an existing sign-in; fresh passwords are generated only for accounts that do not exist yet. To rerun, move or delete the old credentials file, then invoke **demo:provision-access** again with your administrator email, a protected password file, and a new credentials path — the exact options are on [the command-line page](/extend/cli).

The packaged demonstration applies the same rule at its own level: **tools/production-demo.sh** skips provisioning while its state directory already holds a credentials file, and a fresh state directory always produces a fresh run with different generated values.

data.heading: Short answers that end at a screen, a command, or a file.
data.summary: Newcomer and operator questions about Kumwe, its demonstration data, and the way the project is built. Each answer links to the page, screen, or command where you can verify it yourself.

items.question: What is Kumwe?
items.body: Kumwe is a content management system and application platform built on PHP 8.5. One governed core serves the public site, the [administrator](/administrator), the client [portal](/portal), the REST API, the command line, MCP tools, and background workers, so authorization, validation, audit, and persistence behave the same on every surface. This documentation site is itself a running Kumwe installation: every page here is a managed content entry you can open and edit through [Content](/content).

items.question: Is Kumwe a CMS or an application platform?
items.body: Both, deliberately. The content side models pages, workflows, media, and navigation as one editable public site — start at [Content](/content). The application side compiles versioned business definitions into governed transactional workspaces with generated records, reports, policies, and integration events — start at [Business applications](/business). Both sides sit behind the same shared services, so learning one workflow explains the behavior you should expect from the other.

items.question: Where are the demonstration passwords?
items.body: Nowhere in the repository or the demonstration data. Profiles never contain a user, password, token, or secret, and the manifest tests enforce that. Credentials are generated at deployment time: the production demonstration script prints a freshly generated administrator sign-in and writes the generated sign-ins for the full demonstration cast — the staff roles and the portal client members — to a credentials file inside its owner-only state directory. [Demonstration access](/start-here/demo-access) explains how to reach each demonstrated role.

items.question: Can I edit the demonstration pages without losing my changes?
items.body: Yes — they exist to be edited. Every page in this site is an ordinary managed entry with typed fields, workflow state, revisions, and audit records. Reconciliation uses a three-way checksum comparison: a released fixture is updated only while it still matches the state Kumwe last applied, so your changes are preserved and reported rather than overwritten by a later release. Make one small edit through [Pages and publishing](/content/pages) and verify it on the public path.

items.question: How do I remove the demonstration data?
items.body: Decide before the first migration. Set **KUMWE_SITE_CONTENT_PROFILE=blank** and **KUMWE_BUSINESS_PROFILE=none** before the first run of **php bin/kumwe database:migrate** to install an empty site with no business examples. Each dataset's selection is frozen the first time it reconciles, and later runs refuse a different profile — changing profiles in place is not a migration or recovery mechanism. The self-contained production demonstration removes its own containers, volumes, and generated secrets with **bash tools/production-demo.sh down**. [Install and start Kumwe](/start-here/getting-started) covers the surrounding installation steps.

items.question: Can I ship my own demonstration profile in a fork?
items.body: Yes — no PHP changes are required to make a well-formed profile selectable. Demonstration data ships as discoverable, versioned profiles: validated JSON manifests under **resources/demo**. A fork adds a school, a farm, or an online shop by dropping a new profile next to the released ones and selecting it with **KUMWE_SITE_CONTENT_PROFILE** or **KUMWE_BUSINESS_PROFILE** before the first migration. Profiles are data-only — never PHP, SQL, or credentials — each carries an integer version raised on any change, and applied business operations are append-only. The released VDM example described in [Business applications](/business) is the reference implementation of the contract.

items.question: Which databases does Kumwe support?
items.body: MariaDB LTS, MySQL 8.4, and PostgreSQL 17 are supported targets, with Redis supplying runtime coordination such as sign-in throttling, disposable caches, and distributed locks; the selected relational database remains authoritative. Migrations are portable, and the pull-request workflow repeats the full production topology on all three database families, so installation behavior must not depend on one dialect. [Install and start Kumwe](/start-here/getting-started) lists the connection variables; [Operate Kumwe](/operate) covers qualifying a release against every supported family.

items.question: How do layouts relate to content types?
items.body: A content type is the contract: a stable handle, a field schema, a workflow reference, and a published version that pins how entries validate. A layout is presentation: the active template renders each type's presented data as a matching public page. This FAQ is a managed entry whose type defines a heading and a list of question-and-answer items; the template turns that structure into the page you are reading. Change fields and lifecycle in [Content models and workflows](/content/models); change public chrome and presentation in [Media, navigation, and presentation](/content/media-navigation).

items.question: What is the portal?
items.body: The portal at [/portal](/portal) is the authenticated surface for ordinary users such as client members. It is deliberately separate from the public site and the [administrator](/administrator): it creates its own session and exposes only trusted contributed routes and generated surfaces. In the demonstration, a client member sees only that organization's quotations, invoices, subscriptions, and domains beside the shared product catalogue. Read [the client portal](/business/portal) for the boundary and [Security, approvals, and portal](/business/security) for how to verify it.

items.question: How do I check that an installation is healthy?
items.body: Check liveness and readiness before opening the user interface: a successfully migrated site keeps its readiness endpoint at HTTP 200 and serves its compiled assets directly. Then complete one small publishing loop — sign in, edit a demonstration page, and confirm the change on its public path from a signed-out browser — so any failure points at one boundary. [Start here](/start-here) walks through that loop; [Operate Kumwe](/operate) lists the production signals worth monitoring.

items.question: How is the project developed and governed?
items.body: Kumwe is built human-led but AI-assisted: a modern CMS built with disciplined engineering and AI acceleration. Governance follows a curated-contribution model — open in purpose and feedback, curated in implementation, so stability and architecture do not drift. Core code moves through a controlled maintainer pipeline in which every change passes the full quality gate: architecture policy, documentation-block completeness, coding-standard and static-analysis checks, and the test suite. [The Kumwe 2 story](/community/kumwe-2) gives the background; [Community](/community) shows where contributions plug in.

items.question: How do I contribute?
items.body: Start with what the project openly welcomes: use cases, testing, demo profiles, extension ideas, documentation, and domain knowledge. Those contributions have a clear place to plug in and shape releases directly. Code changes travel the curated maintainer pipeline: read the coding standard, then run **composer qa** before submitting — it runs the architecture policy, the documentation-block check, the code-style check, static analysis, and the unit tests. [Community](/community) lists the current entry points.

items.question: Where do I report problems?
items.body: For a suspected security vulnerability, never open a public issue: use the repository's private security-advisory reporting on GitHub and include the affected version, required privileges, exact reproduction steps, and observed impact. For everything else — bugs, documentation gaps, demonstration problems, and ideas — open an issue in the repository's public tracker. [Community](/community) explains how reported feedback feeds the curated-contribution model.

data.heading: Tour the installed VDM business example from catalogue to ledger.
data.summary: The default installation ships the Vast Development Method example: a fictional Namibian software, carpentry, and infrastructure business modelled as twelve typed definitions with sixty-one records, real workflows, derived access policies, and a client portal view. This handbook walks the whole graph and shows where to verify each claim.
data.body:
Keep the default business profile and every fresh installation carries the Vast Development Method (VDM) example: a fictional client-delivery and commerce graph for a Namibian software, carpentry, and infrastructure business. It lives in resources/demo/business/vdm as data-only JSON — profile.json, one typed definition per file under definitions, records.json, and access.json — and installs through the same application services an operator uses, so policies, revisions, audit entries, and idempotency rows exist from the first sign-in. No profile ever contains a password, token, or secret.

## Read alongside this handbook
- [Business definitions](/business/definitions) for the modelling contract behind every schema here.
- [Business records](/business/records) for day-to-day record operations.
- [Security, approvals, and portal](/business/security) for the deny-by-default model this dataset demonstrates.
- [Demo access](/start-here/demo-access) for the generated staff and client sign-ins.

To follow along live, sign in at [/administrator](/administrator) as a staff account from the credentials file and at [/portal](/portal) as a client member, then compare what each surface shows for the same records.

sections.heading: Twelve definitions, one dependency graph
sections.body:
Open **Business definitions** in the administrator and you find the twelve VDM schemas installed in dependency order, every handle prefixed with site.default.vdm_. Half describe consultancy delivery, half describe commerce, and two of them are line definitions owned by their parent documents:

- **Client accounts** — five fictional companies, from Desert Bloom Foods in Windhoek to Copper Ridge Logistics in Otjiwarongo, with contact, service-tier, and status fields.
- **Service catalogue items** — the six offered services that engagements and work entries link to.
- **Engagements** — five delivery agreements binding a client to catalogue services, with an activate, pause, and complete workflow.
- **Service requests** — six inbound requests that are triaged, scheduled, resolved, and closed.
- **Work entries** — eight time and delivery records that are submitted, then approved or rejected.
- **Products** — the ten-item commerce catalogue described in the next section.
- **Quotations** and **quotation lines** — five offers whose ordered lines form an owned collection: a line exists only inside its quotation.
- **Invoices** and **invoice lines** — five billing documents that relate to their client and engagement, link back to an originating quotation, and own their lines the same way.
- **Subscriptions** — five recurring services carrying an exact amount, billing cycle, and renewal date.
- **Domains** — six registered zones with registrar, expiry, and renewal state.

Inspect any one of them to see the complete contract from [business definitions](/business/definitions) in force: typed fields with exact NAD money values, declared relationships, views, actions, workflow bindings, and explicit administrator, portal, and public exposure.

sections.heading: One product catalogue spans goods and services
sections.body:
The catalogue is deliberately mixed so a single definition proves that goods and services share one contract. The product kind field allows physical good, carpentry service, software licence, and hosting service; the billing unit allows each, hour, month, and year; the unit price is exact NAD money. The ten records span:

- **Furniture goods** — the Acacia Study Chair, Karas Council Chair, Omaruru Workshop Table, and Baobab Boardroom Table, priced per item.
- **Carpentry work** — the Built-in Wall Cupboard as a fixed-price build and the Custom Carpentry Hour billed by the hour.
- **Software** — the Nara Inventory Suite Licence and the Field Survey Application Licence, billed per year.
- **Hosting and domains** — Managed Application Hosting per month and Domain Registration and Care per year.

The recurring items do not stop at the catalogue. Subscription records carry the billing cycle, exact amount, start and renewal dates, and an auto-renew flag, so hosting and domain care bill on each renewal rather than through a one-off invoice line; domain records hold the registrar and expiry dates that drive those renewals. Because the product definition uses the open access mode, this catalogue is the one dataset that staff and portal members browse identically.

sections.heading: Documents move through explicit workflow states
sections.body:
Quotations and invoices are workflow documents, not status columns. A quotation starts in draft, moves to sent, and ends accepted, declined, or expired. Send and expire are staff transitions; accept and decline are declared portal actions, so a signed-in client member decides the offer from [/portal](/portal) — and the shipped dataset leaves one quotation pending so you can accept it as the Desert Bloom member.

An invoice starts in draft and is issued by staff. From issued it is either paid through the record-payment transition or marked overdue; an overdue invoice is settled to paid or written off. Write-off is flagged **high-impact**: it demands the independent approval and fresh step-up proof described in [security](/business/security), and it is never exposed to the portal. The shipped ledger holds paid, issued, and overdue examples — including one invoice that went overdue and was then settled — and deliberately writes nothing off, leaving the high-impact path for you to exercise yourself.

The supporting records follow the same pattern. Subscriptions pause, resume, cancel, or lapse; domains are flagged expiring, then renewed or released. Releasing a domain is the profile's second high-impact action. Every transition you replay lands in the record's history and audit trail, which you can inspect from the **Business** area in [/administrator](/administrator).

sections.heading: Four record-access modes decide what the portal sees
sections.body:
The profile manifest assigns each definition one of four record-access modes, and the installer derives closed policy documents from each definition's own field ceilings, installing them with provenance checkpoints so you can trace every rule back to the profile:

- **Open** — a constant allow. Products use it, so every authenticated surface shares one catalogue.
- **Organization** — portal members reach only rows whose organization field equals their authenticated organization, for reading and for declared workflow actions. Quotations, subscriptions, and domains use it, which is why a member can accept a quotation or renew a domain — but only their own.
- **Organization-read** — the same row scope narrowed to reading alone. Invoices, invoice lines, and quotation lines use it: a member studies every line of an invoice yet cannot transition it.
- **Administration** — an appended deny row vetoes every organization context. Client accounts, the service catalogue, engagements, service requests, and work entries never appear in the portal at all.

Organization-less contexts — the administrator, CLI, and API tokens — keep full row visibility, still bounded by each actor's capabilities. The mode only admits rows: which operations exist at all is decided by the definition's closed portal allow-list, in which no flag ever implies another operation. Sign in as a client member from the [demo access](/start-here/demo-access) credentials file and verify the sum: the shared products, your organization's documents, and nothing else. [The client portal](/business/portal) explains the session boundary behind this, and [provision a client](/business/provision-client) shows how to add an organization of your own.

sections.heading: An append-only, byte-immutable ledger keeps the tour reproducible
sections.body:
The dataset is a ledger, not a snapshot. records.json declares every create, relation, workflow action, and archive as an explicit operation with a stable fixture key and an idempotency key, and profile.json fixes the execution order plus the expected totals: twelve definitions, sixty-one records, ninety-six relations, fifty workflow actions, and two archives. Installation replays those operations through the ordinary application services, so the revisions, audit entries, and idempotency rows you inspect are real, not seeded shortcuts.

The release contract is append-only and byte-immutable. The first run of php bin/kumwe database:migrate freezes the profile choice in a durable ledger; later runs refuse a different profile, a manifest downgrade, or a same-version byte change. A released fixture is never edited, reordered, or removed — the profile evolves only by appending operations under a raised version number. Run bash tools/production-demo.sh and you get exactly this graph on every fresh state directory; run it with the down argument to remove the isolated stack again. Your own edits on top are ordinary operator work, cleanly separated from the released fixtures — which is why every count and state in this handbook is something you can check on your own installation.

data.heading: See the business application exactly as one client organization sees it.
data.summary: Sign in at /portal as a fictional client member, read the navigation your grants produce, browse only your organization's quotations and invoices, answer a quotation, and confirm that structural controls are absent by design.
data.body:
The portal is the authenticated surface for ordinary members at [/portal](/portal), intentionally separate from the public site and the administrator. It reuses the shared identity, membership, capability, policy, approval, audit, and business-record boundaries without reusing an administrator session, so what a client member can reach is decided by the same rules you configured in [security and approvals](/business/security) — evaluated from the client's side.

Run this guide against the demonstration stack with demo access provisioned. The fictional client organizations and their generated sign-ins come from the credentials file described in [demo access](/start-here/demo-access).

steps.heading: Find your portal credentials
steps.body: The demonstration provisioning step writes every generated sign-in to demo-access-credentials.json inside the owner-only state directory of tools/production-demo.sh. Alongside the five staff accounts it lists the portal members of three fictional client organizations: two contacts for Kalahari Health Systems and one each for Desert Bloom Foods and the Namib Learning Collective. Each password is generated for your deployment and appears in no profile or repository file. [Demo access](/start-here/demo-access) explains the file and the full cast.

steps.heading: Sign in at the portal
steps.body: Open [/portal](/portal) and sign in with a client member's email and generated password. The server-side context resolver chooses your current site membership and workspace; the optional workspace field on the form is only a bounded hint and can never establish an organization, role, or authority claim. Unknown, ambiguous, and inactive selections receive the same response as invalid credentials, so failed attempts disclose nothing. After login the shell names the server-selected site, organization, and workspace, and the session lives in a portal-only cookie with Path=/portal. The same identity is refused at [administrator](/administrator) sign-in.

steps.heading: Read the Business records navigation
steps.body: The navigation is capability filtered on the server: one card per business definition that your grants and record policy expose, served below /portal/business. A client member sees the shared product catalogue beside the organization's quotations, invoices, subscriptions, and domains. The consultancy records — client accounts, engagements, service requests, and work entries — do not appear, because their record access is administration-scoped. Hiding a link is usability only; the route and application authorization behind it remain mandatory either way.

steps.heading: Browse your organization's quotations and invoices
steps.body: Open the quotations list, then the invoices list. Every row belongs to your organization: each record carries a portal organization identifier that scopes it to one client's members, and the installed record-access policy resolves rows against your current membership, so another client's documents are never listed, counted, or searchable. Requesting another organization's record directly returns the same not-found response as a record that does not exist. Compare the invoice list closely — the fixtures include paid, issued, and overdue examples.

steps.heading: Accept or decline a quotation
steps.body: Sign in as the Desert Bloom Foods member and open the pending quotation in its sent state. The detail offers **Accept quotation** and **Decline quotation**, the two workflow actions the definition marks for the portal. Accepting moves the record from sent to accepted inside the shared record transaction, with authorization, validation, workflow, revision, and audit applied atomically. Send and expire remain administrator-only actions, so a client can answer a quotation but never issue or expire one.

steps.heading: View invoice lines through the relation view
steps.body: From an invoice detail, follow the **Invoice lines** relationship. Each disclosed relationship has its own fixed relation route that hydrates exactly that one handle, so the lines load as a dedicated view. The invoice definition exposes browse, read, relation, history, report, export, and status to the portal — no create, update, or archive — and the line records are organization-read, so quantities and money arrive as exact canonical values you can inspect but not alter.

steps.heading: Understand why structural controls are absent
steps.body: Nothing in the portal edits structure. There is no definition designer, grant editor, workflow toggle, or exposure setting; the only security screen manages your own sign-in credentials. The client member role holds record capabilities plus portal access and nothing wider, the portal operation allow-list defaults to empty, and an exposed view or action never implies another mutation. Policy denial is omission rather than a disabled control, so absence itself is evidence that the boundary holds. Structure stays in the administrator, authored through [business definitions](/business/definitions) and governed as described in [security and approvals](/business/security).

outcome.heading: What you proved
outcome.body: You have exercised multi-tenant isolation from the outside: a shared identity resolved to one exact membership, navigation reduced to the definitions your grants and record policy expose, lists that only ever contain your organization's rows, one permitted workflow action, and a read-only relation view — with every structural control absent by design. To stand up an organization like this yourself, follow [provision a client](/business/provision-client); to compare the same records from the staff side, return to [business records](/business/records).

data.heading: Create the same client through the administrator, the REST API, and MCP.
data.summary: One client needs an active user account, the portal access grant, an organization, and a live membership. This guide produces those four facts in the administrator, over the REST API, and through MCP, automates them with demo:provision-access, and verifies the result at the portal sign-in.
data.body:
A client is not one record. Kumwe admits someone to the portal only when four separate facts line up: an active user account, the portal.access capability, an organization, and a live membership binding that account to the organization. [Business security](/business/security) decides each fact through the same deny-by-default gateway on every surface.

This guide reaches the same provisioned client three ways — through the administrator screens, over the REST API, and through MCP — and then proves the result by signing in at [the portal](/portal). Because every surface calls the same shared application services, each route produces the same memberships, the same optimistic versions, and the same audit events. Where a surface refuses part of the work, that refusal is a designed safeguard, and this guide names it instead of working around it.

steps.heading: Know what a client is made of
steps.body:
Provisioning succeeds when all four facts exist:

- An **active user account**: the shared human identity that signs in at the portal.
- A **portal access grant**: the portal.access capability, carried by a group the account belongs to.
- An **organization**: the business scope the client works inside, optionally divided into workspaces.
- A **live membership**: the versioned binding between the account and the organization; the portal context resolver offers only current memberships.

Miss any one and portal login fails without disclosing which fact was missing, because authentication failures are deliberately non-enumerating. [The portal](/business/portal) page explains the session and context boundary; this guide concentrates on producing the four facts.

steps.heading: Provision in the administrator
steps.body:
Sign in at [the administrator](/administrator) and open **Users and access**. Create the user with an initial password and active status, create or reuse a client group, assign the user to it, and add the portal.access grant to the group. Identity work here requires users.manage, the group review screen confirms the submitted capability change set with a current authenticator or recovery code, and the server repeats every authorization check regardless of what the navigation shows.

Then open the security administration screen, which requires business.security.manage. It manages organizations, workspaces, memberships, and membership roles through typed, allowlisted controls — there is no raw JSON, SQL, or expression editor. Create the client organization, add a workspace if the workflow needs one, and create the membership that binds the new account to the organization with its own version, status, and role assignments. The server blocks self-assignment, stale form versions, and changes outside the selected organization and workspace, and every change produces a redacted audit event.

steps.heading: Provision over the REST API
steps.body:
The identity family under [the REST API](/extend/rest-api) does the same work for integrations. Every request carries a bearer token in the Authorization header plus exactly one Kumwe-Site header naming the site recorded on the token — the security context is never derived from Host or forwarding headers. All identity routes require users.manage, and every mutation requires a caller-generated Idempotency-Key so an identical retry replays the stored response instead of repeating the work.

- **POST /api/v1/users** creates the account with its status; later updates through PATCH carry the current optimistic version.
- **POST /api/v1/roles** creates the client group, and **PUT /api/v1/users/{id}/roles/{roleId}** assigns the user to it.
- **POST /api/v1/roles/{id}/grants** adds the scoped portal.access grant to the group.
- **POST /api/v1/tokens** issues a capability-scoped token when the client also needs machine access; the plaintext appears exactly once in the creation response and never in lists.

The documented REST identity family covers accounts, groups, grants, and tokens. Organization and membership administration remains on the security administration screen, so complete that fact in the browser — the shared services hold that boundary, not the client.

steps.heading: Drive and confirm it over MCP
steps.body:
Connect over authenticated Streamable HTTP with the same bearer token and Kumwe-Site header, or launch a local stdio server with mcp:serve, its required site option, and a protected token file; [MCP](/extend/mcp-server) documents both transports. Each tool then requires its own capability, exactly as the matching screen or endpoint does.

- **kumwe_user_list** lists users, groups, and assignments under users.manage, so a connected client can confirm the account and its group assignment exist.
- **kumwe_token_list** and **kumwe_token_revoke** inspect the client's issued credentials and withdraw them immediately when the task ends.
- **kumwe_business_discover** and **kumwe_business_read** show exactly which generated entities and records a token's bound membership exposes — issue the client a scoped token and the preview is the client's own view.

What MCP will not do is part of the proof: operations that would transmit a password or grant permissions are intentionally not MCP tools, so account creation and the portal.access grant cannot be scripted through a model client. That gap is the same service policy you meet everywhere else — an operation's safeguards travel with the service, and a surface that cannot supply them does not receive the operation.

steps.heading: Let the demonstration provision it for you
steps.body:
The demonstration dataset automates exactly this sequence. The demo:provision-access command reads the selected business profile's access manifest and provisions the whole cast — the accountant, clerk, bookkeeper, stockkeeper, and system administrator staff roles, plus the portal client organizations with their members. It requires host access and a real administrator's credentials: pass the administrator email, an absolute protected password file, and a path for a new credentials file.

The command generates a fresh password for every account it creates and writes them once to an owner-only credentials file it refuses to overwrite. The run is idempotent — already-provisioned identities are confirmed without a password change, so a rerun never invalidates anyone's sign-in. Profiles themselves never contain a password; the credentials file is the only place the generated secrets exist besides the command's own output. [Demo access](/start-here/demo-access) explains how the packaged demonstration uses this file, and [the command line](/extend/cli) documents the full command and its flags.

steps.heading: Verify at the portal sign-in
steps.body:
Sign in at [the portal](/portal) with the new client's credentials. Portal login accepts the shared identity, then the server-side context resolver must find a current membership — the membership you just created. Success creates an opaque portal-only session bound to the site, organization, workspace, membership version, and policy generation, and the shell shows the server-selected context beside capability-filtered navigation.

Test the negative space too. An account without portal.access, a suspended membership, or a stale workspace hint receives the same non-enumerating response as invalid credentials. Inside, the member should see only their organization's records beside anything deliberately shared — in the demonstration dataset a client member sees their own quotations, invoices, subscriptions, and domains beside the shared product catalogue, and nothing belonging to another organization. Administrator visibility is not evidence that portal policy is correct; this sign-in is the test that counts.

outcome.heading: One service, three doors.
outcome.body: The administrator screens, the REST endpoints, and the MCP tools never reimplement provisioning — each one calls the same shared identity and business-security services under the same deny-by-default gateway, producing the same memberships, versions, and audit events. That is why the routes agree: create the account in the browser, add the grant over REST, confirm the result over MCP, and the portal cannot tell the difference. It is also why they deliberately differ at the edges — MCP will not carry a password, the documented REST surface leaves membership administration to the security screens, and only demo:provision-access writes generated credentials to a protected file — because safeguards belong to the operation, not the surface. Whichever door you use, verify from another one: [the records](/business/records) in the administrator, the catalogue over MCP, and the client's own view at [the portal](/portal).

data.heading: Automate every governed workflow through /api/v1.
data.summary: Bearer tokens, explicit site context, idempotent mutations, optimistic versions, and policy-filtered business surfaces give integrations exactly the same authority rules as every interactive screen.
data.body:
The versioned API is rooted at /api/v1, and its authoritative machine-readable contract is the deterministic OpenAPI 3.1 document served at GET /api/v1/openapi.json with a strong entity tag. Generate clients and validation fixtures from that contract rather than scraping rendered documentation, and treat undocumented response fields as unstable.

Every route family shares one discipline: a bearer token with an exact site header, capability checks on both the route and the workflow action, a caller-generated idempotency key on every mutation, and optimistic versions with entity tags on versioned resources. The same application services drive the [command line](/extend/cli) and [MCP tools](/extend/mcp-server), so behavior you verify here predicts those surfaces, and [Security, approvals, and portal](/business/security) explains why a business response may silently omit data another role can see.

This reference concentrates on authentication, content, generated business records, and the shared request contract. The remaining families follow the same conventions under their own capabilities: menus and menu items require navigation.manage; users, groups, grants, and tokens require users.manage; site settings require settings.manage; extension lifecycle requires extensions.manage; schedules and jobs require automation.manage; and the non-executable plan preview at POST /api/v1/plans requires content.read plus an idempotency key.

entries.body: Send the opaque token issued by the administrator or the token:create command as a bearer credential, together with exactly one canonical Kumwe-Site header. The header value must exactly match the site recorded on the token; Kumwe never derives this security context from Host or forwarded proxy headers. Tokens are stored as SHA-256 digests, may expire, and carry an explicit capability set plus bindings for organization or workspace, membership version, policy generation, subject security epoch, audience, purpose, family, and bounded delegation depth. A valid digest is refused when any binding is stale or the requested route has no concrete matching scope, and disabled or deleted sites fail authentication immediately.
entries.example:
GET /api/v1/content HTTP/1.1
Host: cms.example.org
Authorization: Bearer TOKEN
Kumwe-Site: corporate

entries.body: Token administration requires users.manage. GET lists token metadata and never includes token material. POST issues a capability-scoped token and returns the plaintext value exactly once, so store it immediately and never log or retry the creation response through an intermediary that records bodies. DELETE /api/v1/tokens/{tokenId} revokes a token immediately. Issuance and rotation may only reduce the caller's effective capabilities, scope, lifetime, audience, purpose, and delegation depth: a token never exceeds the actor or delegated boundary that created it.
entries.example:
POST /api/v1/tokens HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer TOKEN
Kumwe-Site: corporate
Idempotency-Key: token-issue-20260812-001
Content-Type: application/json

entries.body: Every mutation requires this caller-generated header. Kumwe persists the request digest and the completed response for 24 hours: an identical retry returns the stored response with Idempotency-Replayed: true, while reuse with different request data, authority, scope, or definition is rejected. Read-only routes, including the business search document, do not consume a key. Never retry a non-idempotent request without the same key and body, and honor Retry-After when a response carries it.
entries.example:
Idempotency-Key: page-create-20260804-001

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Idempotency-Replayed: true

entries.body: Reads and mutation results return an entity tag. Updates and deletes of versioned content, menus, and menu items require that latest ETag in If-Match; business record mutations require exactly one strong tag of the form "vN"; user updates instead carry their positive optimistic version inside the JSON document. A stale value produces a precondition or conflict response and never overwrites current state, so read the resource again, reconcile your change, and resend it with the fresh tag.
entries.example:
PATCH /api/v1/content/CONTENT_ID HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer TOKEN
Kumwe-Site: corporate
If-Match: "v3"
Idempotency-Key: page-edit-20260812-002

entries.body: GET lists content and requires content.read. POST creates a draft under content.create, naming the content type, title, slug, and typed data document. GET /api/v1/content/{id} returns one record with its current entity tag. PATCH updates only the supplied fields under content.update, DELETE moves the record to trash under content.delete, and POST /api/v1/content/{id}/restore brings archived or trashed content back under content.restore. Route authorization and workflow authorization both apply: a token holding content.read cannot publish merely because it can reach a transition route. The editorial model behind these records is described in [Pages and publishing](/content/pages).
entries.example:
curl --request POST https://cms.example.org/api/v1/content \ --header "Authorization: Bearer $KUMWE_TOKEN" \ --header 'Kumwe-Site: corporate' \ --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --header 'Idempotency-Key: page-create-20260804-001' \ --data '{"content_type":"page","title":"About us","slug":"about-us","data":{"body":"

About our team.

"}}'

entries.body: One route drives the workflow pinned to the record: submit, review, publish, unpublish, or archive by posting the target status. Authorization is action-specific and follows the same capability map as the administrator; entering a public state always requires content.publish and leaving one always requires content.unpublish. Send the record's current entity tag in If-Match and a fresh idempotency key, then keep the ETag returned by each response for the next versioned mutation.
entries.example:
curl --request POST https://cms.example.org/api/v1/content/CONTENT_ID/transition \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $KUMWE_TOKEN" \
  --header 'Kumwe-Site: corporate' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --header 'Idempotency-Key: page-review-20260804-001' \
  --header 'If-Match: "v1"' \
  --data '{"status":"review"}'

entries.body: Content model definitions are site-scoped and versioned. Reads require content.read; publishing a new definition version requires content.update, the current entity tag in If-Match, and an idempotency key. A content-type schema uses the supported JSON Schema subset in the OpenAPI contract. A workflow contains named states, exactly one non-public initial state, public-state flags, and directed transitions that each demand a capability. Existing content stays pinned to the definition versions that validated it, and a breaking change is rejected unless you explicitly supply allow_breaking: true; that override publishes a new version and never mutates historical ones. Model the change deliberately first — [Content models and workflows](/content/models) explains the editorial consequences.
entries.example:
PATCH /api/v1/content-types/{id} HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer TOKEN
Kumwe-Site: corporate
If-Match: "v2"
Idempotency-Key: page-type-v3-20260812-001
Content-Type: application/json

entries.body: Discovery for generated business surfaces. The collection route returns the definitions, fields, views, actions, and relations visible to your token; GET /api/v1/business/definitions/{definition} inspects one visible generated schema.
