Every result is filtered by the same row, field, and action plan used by the administrator, portal, CLI, and MCP, and denial is omission: a definition or field you may not see is simply absent, and missing and denied record, relation target, approval, and operation identifiers are indistinguishable. Published, actively installed definitions share one stable generic route family, so a new business application needs no new client code.
entries.example:
GET /api/v1/business/definitions HTTP/1.1
Host: cms.example.org
Authorization: Bearer TOKEN
Kumwe-Site: corporate

entries.body: One route family covers the record lifecycle. GET browses and POST creates against the collection; GET, PATCH, and DELETE address one record at /api/v1/business/records/{definition}/{record}; POST to the archive and restore routes changes lifecycle state; GET on the history route reads a bounded revision window; POST to actions/{action} executes a published policy-visible action; and the relations routes browse, add, remove, and reorder targets. Create accepts a values object with record_id set to null; update sends only values. Exact decimals travel as JSON strings, and money and quantity are closed amount-and-currency and amount-and-unit objects. Every mutation requires an idempotency key and, for existing records, exactly one strong If-Match, while GET /api/v1/business/operations/{operation} reads back the caller-bound completed mutation result.
entries.example:
POST /api/v1/business/records/{definition} HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer TOKEN
Kumwe-Site: corporate
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: record-create-20260812-001

{"values":{"total":{"amount":"199.00","currency":"EUR"}},"record_id":null}

entries.body: The bounded read-only query document for a definition's collection. The closed GeneratedBusinessQuery schema accepts a recursive filter, a term-and-fields search, sorts, an opaque after cursor, a page size up to 200, field and include projections, lifecycle flags, and aggregates. Unknown keys, floats for exact values, more than five sorts, 64 filter operations, eight nesting levels, two relation hops, 64 projected fields, four includes, or 16 aggregates are rejected before repository access, and an include is additionally capped at 1,000 hydrated rows and never performs one query per source record. Search is read-only and does not consume an idempotency key, so retry it freely.

GET /api/v1/business/approvals and GET /api/v1/business/approvals/{approval} expose scoped, redacted approval projections: output omits requester, approver, role, policy, payload, and binding digest identities, and a request stays visible only while its active definition still declares the bound high-impact action for the API surface. Bearer REST cannot manufacture the fresh session-bound step-up proof required to approve, reject, or revoke, and a bearer-originated request cannot later be consumed through REST either — complete high-impact execution through the [administrator](/administrator) or [portal](/portal) decision flow. A typed custom action carries the same contract-validated input object into approval and attempted execution; changing that input invalidates the binding, and reusing the operation key for another input is rejected. Ordinary actions remain fully available through REST. The governance model is explained in [Security, approvals, and portal](/business/security).
entries.example:
POST /api/v1/business/records/{definition}/{record}/actions/{action}/approval HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer TOKEN
Kumwe-Site: corporate
Idempotency-Key: action-approval-20260812-001

entries.body: Every failure body is an application/problem+json document carrying type, title, status, and detail, plus the request correlation identifier for support and audit matching. Expect 400 for malformed input, 401 for authentication failure, 403 for a missing capability, 404 for an absent resource, 409 for in-progress or retry conflicts, 412 for stale entity tags, 413 for an oversized request, and 422 for validation failure. Treat undocumented response fields as unstable, honor Retry-After when present, and never retry a non-idempotent request without the same idempotency key and body. An unexpected current-contract invariant failure on the OpenAPI route returns a no-store 503 with Retry-After: 30.

data.heading: Connect model clients to the same governed services as every other surface.
data.summary: The MCP server publishes an explicit, capability-scoped tool catalog over authenticated streamable HTTP and local stdio; every mutation is idempotent, versioned, and audited.
data.body:
This reference describes the MCP surface: how a client connects and authenticates, what each tool or tool group does, and how every call is authorized. After connecting, call the discovery tool and compare its answer with this page.

Give a client only the capabilities required for the immediate task, prefer read-only tokens for analysis and separate short-lived tokens for approved writes, and rotate or revoke the token when the task ends. The [REST API](/extend/rest-api) remains the complete machine-to-machine API, the [command line](/extend/cli) covers operator tasks including the MCP transport, and [Security, approvals, and portal](/business/security) explains the policy model every call passes through.

entries.body: Kumwe exposes capability-protected application services through the official PHP MCP SDK. One server runs over authenticated streamable HTTP and local stdio, and its handlers call the same application services as the administrator, [REST API](/extend/rest-api), and [command line](/extend/cli); they do not query tables, edit files, or bypass workflow, authorization, revisions, optimistic versions, or audit records. High-risk operations that would transmit a password, install an arbitrary package, delete state, or grant permissions are intentionally not MCP tools. Use the administrator, protected CLI, or REST endpoint with the operation's explicit safeguards.

Send a Kumwe bearer token on every request together with the required Kumwe-Site header. That header selects exactly one validated site and must match the site bound into the token; host and forwarding headers never select the site. The transport also validates the exact host, Origin behavior, MCP protocol version, request body limit, and persistent session. The route requires authentication, and each tool then requires its own capability, so a settings-only token can use settings tools without also receiving content access.
entries.example:
POST https://cms.example.org/mcp
Authorization: Bearer TOKEN
Kumwe-Site: corporate

entries.body: For a local client, create a short-lived, least-privilege token and store it in an absolute owner-readable file, then configure the client to launch the stdio server. The required site option selects exactly one site for the lifetime of the process, and the token must have been issued for that same site; a token for another site is rejected. Stdio grants no implicit local administrator power: the token is reverified for expiry, revocation, and its current capabilities before each protected handler access. Run the process as a dedicated unprivileged service account, and never give an MCP client database-administration credentials, signing private keys, backup keys, or unrestricted extension or media filesystem access.
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe mcp:serve \
  --site=corporate \
  --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-mcp-token

entries.body: **kumwe_discover** lists the tools, resources, and prompts exposed to the authenticated token, and the kumwe://capabilities resource returns the machine-readable server surface. The **kumwe_site_review** prompt prepares a content, SEO, structure, or extension review using authorized tools. Neither discovery nor the prompt grants capabilities, and neither can expand the token's access.
entries.example:
kumwe_discover {} -> exposed tools, resources, prompts
read kumwe://capabilities -> machine-readable server surface

entries.body: **kumwe_content_list** (content.read) lists content, optionally including trashed records. **kumwe_content_create** (content.create) creates a draft page, and **kumwe_content_update** (content.update) updates title, slug, and body at an expected version. **kumwe_content_transition** submits, reviews, publishes, unpublishes, archives, or restores through workflow policy; one tool accepts several target states, but each transition performs action-specific authorization. Publishing and unpublishing are audited with the bearer-token subject, and the records you change are the same managed pages described in [Pages and publishing](/content/pages).
entries.example:
kumwe_content_update {
  "title": "Launch update",
  "slug": "launch-update",
  "body": "...",
  "version": 4,
  "operationId": "content-launch-update-01"
}

entries.term: Menu, settings, access, and automation tools
entries.body: **kumwe_menu_list**, **kumwe_menu_create**, **kumwe_menu_item_list**, **kumwe_menu_item_get**, **kumwe_menu_item_create**, **kumwe_menu_item_update**, and **kumwe_menu_item_delete** (navigation.manage) read typed, nested menu items, link content, sections, or safe URLs while maintaining menu paths, and delete a versioned menu item. **kumwe_settings_get** and **kumwe_settings_update** (settings.manage) read browser-managed site settings and update validated identity, homepage, primary menu, schemes, and interaction styles. **kumwe_user_list** (users.manage) lists users, groups, and assignments, while **kumwe_token_list** and **kumwe_token_revoke** inspect token metadata or revoke access. **kumwe_extension_list** and **kumwe_extension_activate** (extensions.manage) list installed extensions and activate one with its runtime map, and **kumwe_schedule_list** and **kumwe_schedule_create** (automation.manage) list schedules or create a validated recurring schedule. Settings changes, extension activation, and schedules are audited with the bearer-token subject.
entries.example:
kumwe_menu_list {} (navigation.manage)
kumwe_settings_get {} (settings.manage)

entries.term: Business definition and schema plan tools
entries.body:
**kumwe_business_definition_list** and **kumwe_business_definition_get** (content.read) list the definition catalog or read a published version, **kumwe_business_definition_draft** and **kumwe_business_definition_history** read the working draft or the published version history, and **kumwe_business_definition_compatibility** previews the compatibility plan the draft would publish. **kumwe_business_definition_publish** (content.update) publishes the draft as a new immutable version at an expected revision.

Schema plan work is deliberately staged. **kumwe_business_schema_definitions** and **kumwe_business_schema_plan_list** (business.schema.read) list plannable definitions or existing plans, and **kumwe_business_schema_plan_get** reads a plan with its durable step journal and canonical checksum. **kumwe_business_schema_plan_create** (business.schema.plan) compiles a deterministic plan and runs no DDL, **kumwe_business_schema_plan_approve** (business.schema.approve) approves the exact inspected checksum, **kumwe_business_schema_plan_execute** (business.schema.execute) applies an approved plan under the schema lock, and **kumwe_business_schema_plan_recover** (business.schema.recover) resumes or reconciles an interrupted plan. Each stage names only its own capability, so a token granted inspection cannot approve, and one granted approval cannot execute; execute and recover are annotated destructive because they change physical tables. Approval binds to the checksum read at inspection, so a plan that changed afterwards is refused rather than applied. Composing a destructive purge plan and approving a high-impact plan both require re-proving the caller's current password, which this surface cannot supply, so those two operations are deliberately absent: use the administrator screen or the protected CLI.
entries.example: plan_create -> plan_get (read checksum) -> plan_approve (bind checksum) -> plan_execute (under schema lock)

entries.body:
Generated records use a bounded static vocabulary; Kumwe never registers a tool for every entity. The current actor's catalog determines which definitions, fields, views, actions, and relations appear. **kumwe_business_discover** lists policy-visible generated entities and capabilities, and **kumwe_business_inspect** inspects one schema, view, action, and relation set. **kumwe_business_search** executes the shared bounded filter, search, sort, and projection document, **kumwe_business_read** reads one record by public identity, and **kumwe_business_history** reads up to 200 policy-filtered revisions before an optional version cursor.

Every write starts with **kumwe_business_plan_mutation**, which seals the proposed mutation to the current actor, scope, policy, definition and runtime generation, input digest, and record version, and returns an opaque five-minute token. **kumwe_business_create**, **kumwe_business_update**, the lifecycle tools **kumwe_business_archive**, **kumwe_business_restore**, and **kumwe_business_delete**, and the relation tools **kumwe_business_relate**, **kumwe_business_unrelate**, and **kumwe_business_reorder** present that token with the exact same arguments; execution re-resolves every binding and fails closed if anything changed. **kumwe_business_request_action** requests maker-checker approval for an exact action binding, **kumwe_business_execute_action** consumes the approved binding when required, and **kumwe_business_operation_status** reads a completed operation only under its original actor, scope, and policy bindings. Results use the same omission-safe projector as [Records and generated surfaces](/business/records) and never include record keys, actor IDs, policy evidence, or denied handles.
entries.example:
1. kumwe_business_plan_mutation { proposed change } -> opaque five-minute plan token
2. kumwe_business_update { same arguments, operationId, plan token, expected version }

entries.body:
Every MCP mutation requires an operationId of 16 to 128 safe characters. Generate one stable ID per intended change and keep it for retries: Kumwe stores the request digest and completed result for 24 hours.

- Retrying the same operation and input returns the stored result.
- Reusing the ID for different input is rejected.
- Retrying while the first operation is running reports an in-progress conflict.
- A failed operation releases the ID so a corrected retry can proceed.

Updates and transitions also require the current positive version; a stale version fails instead of overwriting another editor or integration. Keep operation IDs and returned versions in the calling workflow so retries remain safe.
entries.example: "operationId": "site-menu-rebuild-2026a", "version": 7 -> retry with both unchanged

entries.body:
Every MCP call answers to the decision chain described in [Security, approvals, and portal](/business/security). The route requires authentication, each tool names its own capability, and MCP tokens use the kumwe-mcp audience and MCP purpose while remaining bound to their live site, organization, workspace, membership version, policy generation, security epoch, token family, and delegation depth. Discovery never expands that authority, and every business-record tool or resource must pass the shared row and field disclosure plan before returning identities, counts, relations, aggregates, or values, exactly as the administrator, portal, and [REST API](/extend/rest-api) do.

Step-up stays in the browser. A bearer MCP context has no fresh single-use step-up proof, and Kumwe does not accept a password or authenticator code through a model tool, so approval voting is intentionally absent. Request maker-checker approval through MCP, decide it through the administrator or portal step-up flow, and complete high-impact execution in the browser; ordinary planned actions remain fully executable through MCP. In the client, require human confirmation before publishing, changing settings, or activating extensions, keep tokens, passwords, personal data, and unpublished bodies out of client logs, and monitor audit events, authentication failures, denied capabilities, and unusual mutation volume.

data.heading: Drive the governed runtime from php bin/kumwe.
data.summary: Every management command calls the same shared services as the administrator, REST API, and MCP tools, with token-scoped authorization, stable JSON output, and meaningful exit codes.
data.body:
Run the CLI from the installed release with the same environment as the web application. **php bin/kumwe list** prints every available command; in the production Compose stack, execute the same invocations inside the app service through the packaged entrypoint. Commands return 0 on success and a non-zero status on invalid input, unavailable dependencies, or failed work, and should run as the unprivileged application service account.

## Authentication
- Every token-authenticated management command requires both **--site=SITE** and **--token-file=PATH**. The selected site is validated and must exactly match the site bound into the token, and the verified token subject becomes the audit actor.
- The token file must be absolute, non-symlinked, and readable only by its owner.
- Migration, bootstrap, worker, and scheduler commands use dedicated internal identities instead of bearer tokens; extension package commands additionally rely on protected host and container access.

Commands that expose business records use the same record and field policy plan as the [REST API](/extend/rest-api), [MCP tools](/extend/mcp-server), workers, and the portal, so a permission you verify here is the permission every other surface enforces.

entries.body: The interactive installer walks a new deployment through Composer or ZIP configuration, runs the database migrations, and creates the owner account in one guided session. Use it for a first installation; scripted deployments run **database:migrate** and **user:create-admin** directly instead. [Install and start Kumwe](/start-here/getting-started) covers the startup sequence around it.
entries.example: php bin/kumwe-install

entries.body:
Applies pending forward-only migrations, then reconciles the configured site-content and business datasets. **KUMWE_SITE_CONTENT_PROFILE** selects a content profile the release ships under resources/demo — this release ships **documentation**, **placeholder**, and **blank** — and **KUMWE_BUSINESS_PROFILE** selects **vdm** or **none**; the boolean alias **KUMWE_BUSINESS_DEMO=true** also selects vdm. **documentation** plus **vdm** is the default; use **blank** plus **none** before migrating a new database for an empty start.

Each dataset's choice is frozen when its first reconciliation passes validation and begins: every later invocation, including production's one-shot migrate service, must receive the same value, and a different value fails instead of switching profiles. Profiles carry no credentials — create administrators, ordinary users, tokens, and passwords through their dedicated commands. Migration holds a database-session advisory lock plus a compatibility row; when upgrading from a build that only used the expiring row lock, stop every older application, worker, and scheduler before migrating.
entries.example:
KUMWE_SITE_CONTENT_PROFILE=documentation \
KUMWE_BUSINESS_DEMO=true \
php bin/kumwe database:migrate

entries.body: Lists pending migrations and returns exit status 2 when work is pending, so a deployment pipeline can gate a release on a clean status without parsing output. Run it before and after **database:migrate** to confirm the schema is where you expect.
entries.example: php bin/kumwe database:status

entries.body: Removes one expired migration lock left behind by a crashed pre-advisory process, after a quiesced cutover. Read the exact owner token from the **migration_locks** table first: the command authorizes the system migration use case, verifies expiry, holds the new advisory namespace, and performs an exact compare-and-delete. It will not clear an active, changed, malformed, or unconfirmed owner. Run **database:migrate** immediately afterward.
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe database:recover-lock \
  --expected-owner=EXACT_64_HEX_OWNER \
  --confirm-legacy-quiesced

entries.body: Checks readiness from the application process. Use it during startup verification and deployment diagnostics before opening the [administrator](/administrator): a passing check means the runtime itself, not just the web server, considers its dependencies available.
entries.example: php bin/kumwe app:health

entries.body: Creates the initial owner account. It requires **--email**, **--name**, and an absolute **--password-file** whose group and other permission bits are clear, so the password never appears on the command line. Remove the password file after use, then sign in at [/administrator](/administrator).
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe user:create-admin \
  --email=owner@example.com \
  --name='Site owner' \
  --password-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-owner-password

entries.body: Provisions the selected business profile's demonstration cast — administrator staff roles such as the accountant, clerk, bookkeeper, stockkeeper, and system administrator, plus the portal client organizations with their members — from the profile's access manifest. It requires host access and a real administrator's credentials, generates a fresh password for every account it creates, and writes them once to an owner-only credentials file it refuses to overwrite. The run is idempotent: already-provisioned identities are confirmed without a password change, so a rerun never invalidates anyone's sign-in. See [demonstration sign-ins](/start-here/demo-access) for where the packaged demo writes this file.
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe demo:provision-access \
  --admin-email=administrator@kumwe.test \
  --admin-password-file=/absolute/protected/password-file \
  --credentials-file=/absolute/new/demo-access-credentials.json

entries.body: Issues a management credential with an explicit capability list and expiry, authorized by an operator password file or an existing token file. The plaintext token is printed exactly once — route it directly to a secret manager and clear terminal capture according to site policy. When the capabilities reach organization-sensitive records, a password-authenticated operator passes **--organization=IDENTIFIER** and, for a workspace-bound credential, also **--workspace=IDENTIFIER**; Kumwe resolves that exact live membership from storage and embeds its membership and policy generations, so the identifiers alone confer no authority, and a workspace without an organization is refused. Issuance authorized by an existing token file cannot override either selection. CLI credentials use the kumwe-cli audience and a closed management purpose, and site, organization, workspace, membership version, policy generation, security epoch, family, and delegation depth are revalidated before a concrete command is authorized.
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe token:create \
  --site=default \
  --email=owner@example.com \
  --name=deployment-integration \
  --capabilities=content.read,content.create,content.update \
  --expires-at=2027-01-01T00:00:00Z \
  --password-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-owner-password

entries.body: Manages users, roles, and grants on one site. **users**, **roles**, and **tokens** list the current identities and credentials; **create-user**, **create-role**, **assign-role**, and **grant** build access up, while **update-user**, **revoke-role**, **revoke-grant**, and **revoke-token** take it away. User updates require the current **--version**. Password files must be absolute, non-symlinked, readable only by their owner, and removed after use. Revoke a leaked API or MCP credential immediately with **access revoke-token**. The capability and scope model these grants feed is described in [security, approvals, and portal](/business/security).
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe access create-user \
  --site=corporate --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-identity-token \
  --email=editor@example.com --display-name='Site editor' \
  --password-file=/run/secrets/editor-initial-password --status=active
php bin/kumwe access grant \
  --site=corporate --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-identity-token \
  --role=ROLE_ID --capability=content.update --scope-type=global

entries.body: Prints JSON and calls the same content service as the administrator, REST API, and MCP tools. **list**, **get**, **create**, **update**, **transition**, **trash**, and **restore** cover the editorial lifecycle; every mutation must send the current returned version, and **--deleted=1** on list includes trashed records when recovery work needs them. The workflow states you move through are the ones described in [pages and publishing](/content/pages).
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe content create \ --site=corporate --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-operator-token \ --title='About us' --slug=about-us --content-type=page \ --data='{"body":"

About our team.

"}' php bin/kumwe content transition \ --site=corporate --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-operator-token \ --id=CONTENT_ID --version=2 --status=review

entries.body: Manages the same site-scoped, immutable content-type and workflow definitions as the administrator and REST API. Set **--kind=content-type** or **--kind=workflow**; **create** takes the complete definition, and **update** requires **--id**, the current positive **--version**, and a full replacement. Pass **--allow-breaking=1** only after deliberately reviewing consumers — historical content remains pinned to its earlier versions. [Content models and workflows](/content/models) explains what the definitions contain.
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe content-model create --kind=content-type \
  --site=corporate --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-content-token \
  --handle=article --name=Article --workflow=WORKFLOW_ID \
  --schema='{"type":"object","properties":{"body":{"type":"string"}},"required":["body"],"additionalProperties":false}'

entries.body: Drives the same versioned business-definition catalog as the administrator and REST API. Reads — **list**, **get**, **draft**, **history**, **compatibility** — require content.read; everything else requires content.update. **import** reads the definition document from a protected file rather than the command line, so a definition never reaches the process table. Inspect **compatibility** before publishing: a plan that changes behavior or data refuses to publish unless you pass **--confirmed=1**. Use **--version** with **get** to read a specific published version, and **supersede**, **deprecate**, or **reject** with **--version** to retire one. Start with [business definitions](/business/definitions) for what a definition declares.
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe business-definition import --site=corporate \
  --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-modeller-token \
  --definition-file=/run/secrets/asset-definition.json
php bin/kumwe business-definition publish --site=corporate \
  --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-modeller-token \
  --handle=site.corporate.asset --expected-revision=4 --confirmed=1

entries.body: Inspects and applies compiled schema plans, with a dedicated capability per stage so inspection, approval, and execution can be held by different operators: **definitions**, **plans**, and **get** need business.schema.read, **plan** needs business.schema.plan, **approve** needs business.schema.approve, **execute** needs business.schema.execute, **recover** needs business.schema.recover, and **purge-plan** needs business.schema.destructive. **get** returns the plan with its durable step journal and canonical checksum, and approval binds to that exact checksum — if the plan changed after you inspected it, approval fails rather than applying something you did not read. High-impact and destructive plans additionally require **--confirmation** and recorded recovery evidence via **--evidence**. After an interrupted execution, inspect the journal first, then use **recover**.
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe business-schema plan --site=corporate \
  --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-schema-token --definition=DEFINITION_ID
php bin/kumwe business-schema approve --site=corporate \
  --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-approver-token \
  --plan=PLAN_ID --expected-checksum=CHECKSUM
php bin/kumwe business-schema execute --site=corporate \
  --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-executor-token --plan=PLAN_ID

entries.body:
Reads and mutates generated business records through the same shared catalog, query decoder, exact-value projector, and transactional record service as every other surface, printing a stable JSON success or error envelope. Actions cover discovery with **entities** and **schema**; reads with **list**, **get**, **history**, **report**, and **export**; lifecycle with **create**, **update**, **archive**, **restore**, and **delete**; custom actions with **action** and **request-action**; relations with **relate**, **unrelate**, and **reorder**; approvals inspection with **approvals** and **approval**; and **operation** status. There is no organization-selection flag — the token's live membership decides scope.

Mutations require a stable **--operation-id**, reused only for an identical retry, and existing-record mutations require the positive **--expected-version** last read. Values, action input, query documents, target values, and reorder lists are accepted only from absolute, owner-only, regular files capped at 2 MiB, so PII and secrets never leak through process lists. The CLI deliberately exposes no approval vote: a high-impact decision still requires the browser's fresh, session-bound step-up proof, while ordinary actions remain fully executable here. Failures carry a redacted error code and stable exit status — 64 usage, 65 malformed data, 66 missing or denied, 69 unavailable, 73 conflict, 75 in progress, 77 authorization, 78 configuration. See [records and generated surfaces](/business/records).
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe business-record list \
  --site=corporate --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-cli-token \
  --definition=acme.sales_order --query-file=/run/kumwe/query.json
php bin/kumwe business-record update \
  --site=corporate --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-cli-token \
  --definition=acme.sales_order --record=SO-00042 \
  --expected-version=7 --operation-id=sales-order-42-update-0008 \
  --values-file=/run/kumwe/order-values.json

entries.body: Manages menus and their items: **list**, **create-menu**, **update-menu**, and **delete-menu** for menus; **items**, **get-item**, **create-item**, **update-item**, and **delete-item** for entries. Target a managed page with **--target-type=content**, a section link with **--target-type=anchor** and a fragment target URL, or a safe custom destination with **--target-type=url**. Updates and deletes require **--id** and **--version**; pass an empty **--parent=** for a root item. The structures you edit here render as described in [media, navigation, and presentation](/content/media-navigation).
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe navigation create-item \
  --site=corporate --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-operator-token \
  --menu=MENU_ID --title=About --slug=about --position=10 \
  --target-type=content --content=CONTENT_ID

entries.body: **get** prints the site's current settings and **update** changes only the options you pass, so presentation options omitted from an update retain their current database values. Alongside the site name, homepage content, locale, timezone, and search indexing, the presentation flags control the logo, primary menu, active scheme, button style and shape, header style, and footer text; **--presentation-schemes-json** replaces the reusable validated scheme list and **--presentation-json** replaces the complete presentation object returned by get. Only browser-managed site settings belong here — change database, Redis, proxy, release, and secret configuration through the deployment environment covered in [Operate Kumwe](/operate).
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe settings update \
  --site=corporate --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-operator-token \
  --site-name='Example site' --homepage-content=CONTENT_UUID \
  --locale=en --timezone=Africa/Windhoek \
  --presentation-active-scheme=corporate --presentation-header-style=glass

entries.body: Manage signed extension packages through their full lifecycle. **extension:install** takes an absolute package path with its **--key-id** and **--signature**; **extension:activate** enables a package, adding **--surface=site** to activate a theme for the public site; **extension:disable** and **extension:uninstall** reverse the process, and **extension:list** shows the current state. These commands additionally rely on protected host and container access. Restart long-running workers after any extension lifecycle change. Packaging and signing are covered in [extensions and templates](/extend/extensions).
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe extension:install /absolute/package.zip \
  --site=corporate --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-extension-token \
  --key-id=KEY --signature=BASE64
php bin/kumwe extension:activate vendor/theme \
  --site=corporate --surface=site \
  --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-extension-token

entries.body: Restores the core administrator theme. The command demands the exact confirmation value shown in the example, so it cannot run by accident; reach for it when an administrator theme activation needs to be rolled back to the shipped interface.
entries.example: php bin/kumwe theme:administrator:recover --confirm=restore-core-administrator

entries.body: Runs a queue worker against a named queue. Use the long-lived form under a supervisor with a polling interval, or **--once** to process a single job as a one-shot deployment diagnostic. Workers use a dedicated internal identity rather than a bearer token, and must be restarted after extension lifecycle changes.
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe queue:work --queue=default --sleep-ms=1000
php bin/kumwe queue:work --once

entries.body: Runs the scheduler that dispatches due automation schedules. Use **--loop** for the long-lived process under a supervisor, or the one-shot form for deployment diagnostics. Like the queue workers, it uses a dedicated internal identity instead of a bearer token.
entries.example: php bin/kumwe schedule:run --loop

entries.body: Manages the schedules and jobs the workers execute. **create** registers a cron-timed job with a name, timezone, job handle, and JSON payload; **schedules** and **jobs** list the current state; **enable**, **disable**, and **delete** take **--id** and **--version**, and **retry** or **cancel** take **--id** for queued jobs. [Integrations and automation](/extend/integrations) describes the jobs themselves.
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe automation create \
  --site=corporate --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-automation-token \
  --name="Nightly extension map" --cron="0 2 * * *" --timezone=UTC \
  --job=extensions.runtime.rebuild --payload='{}'
php bin/kumwe automation schedules \
  --site=corporate --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-automation-token

entries.body: Serves the MCP stdio transport: the command reads MCP frames from standard input and writes protocol output to standard output, so an agent client launches it directly. **--site** is required and the protected token must have been issued for that exact site; the token determines the tool capabilities, and local shell access does not imply owner access. Run it under a dedicated service account with no database-administration or unrestricted host-filesystem access. The tools it exposes are documented in [MCP](/extend/mcp-server).
entries.example:
php bin/kumwe mcp:serve \
  --site=corporate \
  --token-file=/run/secrets/kumwe-mcp-token

data.heading: Open in purpose, curated in implementation.
data.summary: Kumwe welcomes use cases, testing, demo profiles, extension ideas, documentation, and domain knowledge; core code moves through a controlled maintainer pipeline so releases stay coherent and safe.
data.body:
Kumwe is a modern CMS and application platform, built human-led with disciplined engineering and AI acceleration. The community works the same way: participation is open in purpose and feedback, and curated in implementation, so the stability and architecture you rely on do not drift.

## What is welcome
- Use cases and feedback from real sites and real operations
- Testing against the released application and its documentation
- Demo profiles that show Kumwe running a new domain
- Extension ideas and packaged extensions
- Documentation corrections and improvements
- Domain knowledge that sharpens definitions and policies

Core code moves through a controlled maintainer pipeline: every change is reviewed and passes the same quality gate before it ships, so each release stays coherent and safe. The sections below explain how the platform is built, why contribution works this way, and exactly where each of those contributions lands.

sections.heading: How Kumwe is built.
sections.body:
Kumwe is built human-led and AI-assisted: maintainers set the architecture, review every change, and own every release, while disciplined tooling and AI acceleration raise the pace without lowering the bar. That discipline is mechanical, not aspirational. One quality gate runs the architecture policy, the coding standard, static analysis at its strictest level, and the test suites on every change. Every class, method, property, constant, and enum case carries a documentation block. Dependencies arrive through constructors, and the dependency direction is enforced by the same gate: domain depends on nothing, and infrastructure and delivery depend inward.

The evidence is this running system. Every guide on this site ends in an observable result — a public page, a governed record, a policy denial, a durable job — because the platform is built so its claims can be checked. [Start here](/start-here) if you have not taken that tour yet.

sections.heading: The curated-contribution model.
sections.body:
Kumwe is open in purpose and feedback, and curated in implementation. Anyone can shape what the platform should do: report what works and what fails, describe the site or operation you need, question a decision, or propose a capability. What stays curated is how those needs become core code. A small maintainer group writes and reviews the core, so the architecture keeps one direction, security boundaries keep one owner, and every release is something the maintainers can stand behind.

The reason is the platform's own promises. Versioned definitions, policy-checked record services, immutable revisions, and guarded schema plans hold only while the code enforcing them stays coherent; a pipeline where every core change passes the same review and the same gate is how those guarantees survive growth. Contribution outside that pipeline is designed to be first-class, not a consolation: demo profiles, extensions, documentation, and testing are all supported surfaces that do not wait on core commit access.

sections.heading: Where you can plug in today.
sections.body:
Each item below lands on a real surface in the released platform.

- **Use cases and feedback.** Describe the site, application, or workflow you need in concrete terms: which records, which actors, which policies, which reports. The vocabulary in [Business definitions](/business/definitions) — fields, exposure, actions, approvals — is the most useful shape for that description.
- **Testing.** Install the release or use the [demo access](/start-here/demo-access) accounts, follow a guide, and report exactly where behavior and documentation disagree. A precise reproduction against a named screen or route is a contribution maintainers can act on immediately.
- **Demo profiles.** Demonstration data ships as drop-in profile directories under resources/demo: a site-content manifest, or a business directory with its profile, definitions, and records documents. A well-formed profile becomes selectable at installation with no PHP changes, so a school, a farm, or an online shop demonstration is something you can build and share today; the released VDM business profile is the reference implementation of the contract.
- **Extensions and extension ideas.** An extension is a versioned package with a kumwe.json manifest at its root, contributing services, routes, business definitions, events, jobs, and templates through typed registries. The small examples shipped under examples/extensions are inspectable starting contracts, and [Extensions and templates](/extend/extensions) documents the format and lifecycle.
- **Documentation.** These pages are managed content, and the repository documentation is plain Markdown. Corrections, missing steps, and clearer explanations are welcome — especially where you tested something and the words did not match the behavior.
- **Domain knowledge.** If you know how bookkeeping, inspections, stock, or membership actually works, that knowledge shapes better definitions, policies, demo profiles, and defaults than code alone can.

sections.heading: How decisions stay coherent.
sections.body:
Every proposal follows the same route, whoever raises it. A need is stated as a use case, weighed against the published architecture principles, and then either scheduled as core work in the maintainer pipeline or directed to a surface that does not need core changes — usually an extension or a demo profile. Core work then passes review, the full quality gate, and the release checks described in [Operate Kumwe](/operate) before it ships.

Two consequences are worth stating plainly. A good idea may land as an extension rather than a core feature; that is the architecture protecting every existing installation, and the extension surface is built to carry real functionality, not leftovers. And a release ships when its behavior, documentation, and recovery story agree, not when a date arrives. [Kumwe 2](/community/kumwe-2) is what that standard most recently produced.

sections.heading: Source, issues, and discussions.
sections.body:
Kumwe lives on GitHub, and that is where every conversation starts.

- [Read the source](https://github.com/kumwe/cms) — the platform, the examples, the demo profiles, and every quality gate are in one repository.
- [Open an issue](https://github.com/kumwe/cms/issues) — precise reproductions, documentation gaps, and use-case descriptions are all welcome issues.
- [Join the discussions](https://github.com/kumwe/cms/discussions) — questions, ideas, demo profiles you are building, and feedback on the direction of the platform.

Meet [the team behind Kumwe](/community/team) to see who reads them.

data.heading: Human-led means humans you can name.

data.body:
Kumwe is a modern CMS and application platform, built with disciplined engineering and AI acceleration — and the discipline has owners. The maintainers named here define the architecture, review every change, validate the quality gates, and stand behind each release. More of the team will be introduced on this page over time.

If you want to work with the team, [Community and contribution](/community) explains where use cases, testing, demo profiles, extension ideas, documentation, and domain knowledge plug in.

sections.heading: Llewellyn van der Merwe — lead architect
sections.body:
Llewellyn is the lead architect of Kumwe: he defines how the platform should work, monitors and validates its quality gates, workflows, and deliverables, and carries the architectural decisions the [curated-contribution model](/community) describes. He is Director and Senior Architectural Engineer of Intelligent Software and Systems at Vast Development Method — the practice whose initials the [business demonstration](/business/handbook) carries.

His engineering record long predates AI-accelerated development. He is a long-standing contributor to the Joomla project and its ecosystem, and the creator of Joomla Component Builder, a definition-driven component generator whose philosophy — declare the model, generate the working software — Kumwe’s typed business platform carries forward. His open-source work spans the getBible platform, official Joomla Docker images and the octojoom tooling, and AI-era bridges such as an MCP server for Joomla site management; it has earned an Arctic Code Vault contribution and GitHub Developer Program membership.

data.heading: Version 2.0 turns the running installation into its own demonstration.
data.summary: Kumwe 2.0 ships six document-driven layouts, a typed business demonstration you can trace end to end, least-privilege security you can test from the client portal, pluggable demo profiles, and generated sign-ins for every demonstrated role.
data.body:
Kumwe 2.0 is a release you can walk through rather than read about. The page in front of you is part of the evidence: an ordinary managed content item, rendered by the new article layout and published through the same workflow, revision, and menu services as every other page on this site. Each capability below ends in a screen, a command, or a file you can open.

## A content engine that documents itself

The managed content engine renders six document-driven layouts — landing, document, guide, reference, questions and answers, and article — each defined by a validated schema and filled by ordinary content items. The homepage demonstrates the landing layout, [the FAQ](/start-here/faq) demonstrates questions and answers, and this article demonstrates the article layout, with its published label, highlights, and further-reading list all supplied by structured fields. Open Content in the [administrator](/administrator) to inspect the fields, revision, publication state, and ownership of any page here, or start from [Content models](/content/models) to see how the layouts are defined.

## A typed business platform, demonstrated end to end

The Vast Development Method (VDM) business demonstration ships twelve related schemas: a consultancy graph plus a commerce graph of products, quotations with ordered lines, invoices, subscriptions, and domain registrations, each with workflows, views, actions, and exposure rules. Inspect the model in [Business definitions](/business/definitions), then use [Business records](/business/records) to trace a fictional client account through its service request, engagement, catalogue service, and work entries — and follow the commerce side from an accepted quotation to its invoice, subscription, and domains, comparing paid, issued, and overdue examples.

## Least privilege you can sign in and test

Authorization in 2.0 is layered: capabilities begin the decision, and site ownership, organization and workspace membership, row policy, field disclosure, maker-and-checker approvals, step-up proofs, and token scope finish it. The client portal proves the model from the outside. It creates its own authenticated context, and a member signing in at [the portal](/portal) sees only that organization's quotations, invoices, subscriptions, and domains beside the shared product catalogue — including accepting a pending quotation as a portal workflow action. [Security, approvals, and portal](/business/security) explains the policy layers, and [the client portal guide](/business/portal) walks the member journey.

## Pluggable demonstration profiles

Demonstration data is no longer hard-coded seeding. A profile is a directory of validated JSON manifests below resources/demo; the demo catalog discovers what a release ships, and operators select the site-content and business datasets independently through the KUMWE_SITE_CONTENT_PROFILE and KUMWE_BUSINESS_PROFILE environment variables. A fork adds its own demonstration — a school, a farm, an online shop — by dropping a well-formed profile next to the released ones, with no PHP changes. Reconciliation is a three-way checksum comparison, so a page you have customized is preserved and reported rather than overwritten by a later release.

## Identities without shared secrets

Run bash tools/production-demo.sh from the repository root and the demonstration provisions its full cast: the accountant, clerk, bookkeeper, stockkeeper, and system administrator staff accounts, plus the portal members of the fictional client organizations. Every sign-in is freshly generated and written to demo-access-credentials.json inside the script's owner-only state directory; Kumwe's profiles never contain a user or password. That one file is how a reviewer enters every demonstrated role — compare what each staff account can reach in the [administrator](/administrator), then switch to a client member in the portal. [Demonstration access](/start-here/demo-access) covers the details, and [provisioning a client](/business/provision-client) shows how to add an organization of your own.

## How this release was built

Kumwe is a new kind of CMS and application platform that's built human-led but AI-assisted. Maintainers own every architectural decision, security boundary, and release gate in 2.0, and acceleration passes through the same review, analysis, and test gates as any other change. The project is open in purpose and feedback and curated in implementation; the [community pages](/community) explain where use cases, testing, demo profiles, extension ideas, and documentation plug in.

Take the tour from [Start here](/start-here), or jump straight to [operating the complete runtime](/operate).
highlights: Six document-driven layouts — landing, document, guide, reference, questions and answers, and article — render every page of this demonstration site from validated, structured content.
The VDM business demonstration ships twelve related schemas spanning a consultancy graph and a commerce graph of products, quotations, invoices, subscriptions, and domain registrations.
Least-privilege authorization layers capabilities, membership, row policy, field disclosure, approvals, step-up proofs, and token scope on every surface.
Client members sign in at the portal and see only their own organization's commerce records beside the shared product catalogue.
Demonstration data ships as discoverable, versioned profiles that forks extend without any PHP changes.
Every demonstration identity is generated at provisioning time; no profile ever contains a user or password.
